When the mandatory training modules come around he books the computer in the staff room and does them after shift, ideally the first one alongside someone who has done it before.
He reads with glasses now and prefers print for anything longer than a screen, and he will print a policy at work rather than read it on the tablet. He talks better than he types. His notes were brief to a fault until the coordinator showed him dictation on the tablet, which he has taken to with enthusiasm and now overuses slightly.
In the falls huddles he is comfortable in front of the wing team, which surprised him. One to one with a nervous new starter he is better again.
sections.additionalInfo:
Gary and Lyn have their two grandchildren every Sunday, non-negotiable. He plays lawn bowls Tuesday evenings and is the unofficial bus for half the team.
His nights block each month means any regular weekly commitment, a class on a set evening for instance, falls over one week in four. He has not sat in a classroom since his Certificate III and describes that experience as "fine once I stopped worrying about it".

learners.name: Amber Roylance
learners.bio: Real estate sales administrator who assembles pre-listing packs, orders title and council searches, wrote the agency's CRM data entry standard, and has twice caught a vendor who was not the registered owner.

sections.aboutMe: Amber Roylance is 27 and rents at Blair Athol with two housemates. She is the sales administration assistant at Bellchambers & Co, a two-office real estate agency at Prospect and Enfield, where she has worked for four years. She is saving hard for her own place, which she describes as "professionally ironic".
sections.professionalExperience:
Amber came to the agency from two years of café and retail work, hired originally as a receptionist. She is now the person who makes listings happen behind the scenes: when an agent wins a property, Amber assembles the pre-listing pack, ordering the title search and the council and easement information through the agency’s search provider, pulling recent comparable sales from the sales data platform, and checking that what the vendor told the agent matches what the records actually say. She has caught two vendors who were not the registered owner, one innocently and one less so.
She keeps the agency’s CRM honest, wrote its one-page data entry standard, and collates the search certificates for the Form 1 packs under the direction of the registered conveyancer. She showed the current receptionist everything the role involves.
No formal qualifications since school beyond her RSA and a barista course. Everything at the agency she learned from the previous administrator in a fortnight of handover, and the rest she worked out.
sections.careerGoals: Amber wants to become a property manager, which in SA means registration and study, and the principal has agreed to support her. First, she wants her current skills recognised so she is not starting from zero, and privately she wants the confidence boost of something on paper, because being self-taught makes her feel like a fraud around the certificated agents, which everyone but Amber can see is unjustified.
sections.workingStyle:
Amber is fast, phone-first, and lives in the CRM, the search portal, and the office chat. She keeps her task list in an app, colour-coded, and turns listing packs around in under 48 hours. Give her a new system and she will be teaching it to others by Friday.

Her confidence dips around money. Trust receipts make her anxious and she double-checks everyone with the property manager before entering it, and percentages and commission splits she quietly recalculates three times. Nobody has ever found an error; the checking is about her, not the numbers.

She works every Saturday morning through open inspection season handling the office, so weekends are broken, and Sundays she shoots photography jobs, her side business. Weekday evenings are her genuinely free time. She reads quickly on a screen, writes in a bright, informal voice that needs a formality pass for anything official, and after years of being the person who makes things happen quietly, she freezes when asked to speak in the Tuesday sales meeting.
sections.additionalInfo: The photography side business is real income: family portraits and the occasional wedding second-shooter gig, edited on Sunday nights. She plays social netball Thursdays. Her laptop is her own and excellent, her home internet is fine, and her preferred way to learn anything is a short video at 1.5 speed followed by immediately doing it herself.

learners.name: Jake Trewartha
learners.bio: Licensed roof plumber running his own three-person business, supervising a second-year apprentice through a group training organisation and twice refusing to sign off a logbook task he judged unready.

sections.aboutMe:
Jake Trewartha is 38 and lives at Semaphore with his partner Ellie and their daughter. He is a licensed roof plumber and runs Trewartha Roofing & Cladding out of a shed at Port Adelaide: himself, another tradesman, and a second-year apprentice named Coop.
The business is small enough that a fortnight of bad weather is felt in the bank account.
sections.professionalExperience:
Jake did his roof plumbing apprenticeship out of Port Adelaide, worked six years for a commercial roofing contractor across warehouses and school re-roofs, then went out on his own in 2016.
The business does residential re-roofs, box gutters, wall cladding, and a steady run of flashing and penetration work for builders and the odd solar and mechanical contractor who has cut a hole in someone's roof and would like it to stop raining inside.
He holds his SA contractor licence for roof plumbing work and supervises Coop through a group training organisation, with the GTO field officer visiting quarterly. Jake does the on-the-job instruction himself and takes it seriously. His own tradesman years, he says, were "learn by getting yelled at", and he runs it differently: he shows a task, watches Coop do it, and comes back to it a week later to see whether it stuck. He signs off Coop's logbook and has twice told the field officer that a task was not ready to be marked off yet.
He has no qualifications beyond his trade certificate and licence, and has never done any study since his apprenticeship.
sections.careerGoals:
The GTO field officer planted the idea. Jake is already training an apprentice to trade standard, and formal recognition would let him take on a second apprentice with more confidence and possibly do paid assessment work for the GTO down the track.
Jake likes the sound of the second apprentice. The business is turning work away from May to September and he is doing more of the physical work himself than he should be at 38. Paid assessment work also appeals as something he could still do at 55.
sections.workingStyle:
Jake's day starts at 6:30 in the shed and ends when the light does. His diary is his phone. Quotes are voice memos recorded in the ute that Ellie turns into written quotes at night, because writing has been a battle since school and he long ago stopped fighting it and built the workaround instead.
He reads plans, specs, and the flashing handbook diagrams fluently. It is composing sentences he avoids, not reading them, and he can pick a detailing error on a drawing that the builder has missed.
He photographs everything. Every job gets before, during, and after shots on his phone, filed by job in a gallery app, partly for disputes and partly because it is how he shows Coop what right looks like. Show him a video and he is engaged; hand him a page of text and he will find something to go and measure.
Rain days are his free time, and there is no predicting them. Anything he commits to has to survive being dropped for a fortnight in a wet June and picked up again without him having to start over. He has a phone and Ellie's iPad; the laptop is technically his but he treats it like it might bite, and it lives in a drawer in the shed.
sections.additionalInfo:
Jake surfs before work when the bank at Semaphore is doing anything, coaches his daughter's under-8s soccer on Saturday mornings in winter, and is the person half the street asks about their gutters.
Ellie does the books, the invoicing, and increasingly the diplomacy. Jake has said that if anything needs to be written down and submitted, Ellie will end up doing it, and he does not seem to think this is a problem.

learners.name: Dean Kovacevic
learners.bio: Pool construction supervisor running two crews and the excavation programme, who writes the site investigation report every quote is built from and has twenty-six years on the tools behind him.
learners.employer: Meridian Pools — metropolitan Adelaide and Fleurieu

sections.aboutMe: Dean Kovacevic is 44 and lives at Golden Grove with his wife and three kids. He is the construction supervisor at Meridian Pools, a family-owned pool builder working across metropolitan Adelaide and down to the Fleurieu, and he runs two crews and the excavation program.
sections.professionalExperience:
Dean started as a concreter's labourer at eighteen, spent eleven years on wet concrete and formwork, then moved to pools in 2012 because a mate said the work was steadier. He has been at Meridian for nine years and supervising for five.
His week is the front end of the build. He does the site investigation on every job before the excavator is booked, which means the soil, the fall and levels, the access, the services, the trees, the neighbours, the easements, and whether the thing the client has drawn on the back of an envelope will actually fit between the house and the fence with the setbacks the council wants.
He writes the site report the office quotes from, sets out the pool, and supervises the dig, standing over the trench and calling the operator off when something appears that should not be there. He deals with the client on the day, which is often the point at which they find out their pool cannot go where they wanted it.
He holds a white card and an excavator ticket, did a soil classification short course through a supplier, and has never done anything else formal. Everything he knows about clay, reactive soils, and what happens when you put a shell next to a paperbark he learned by getting it wrong early and expensively.
sections.careerGoals:
The owners are talking about Dean stepping up to construction manager when Rob retires in two or three years, and the accountant has pointed out that the company's building work licence sits with Rob personally.
Dean needs a qualification behind him for the licence question, not for the job itself, which he is already doing. He is pragmatic about it and mildly annoyed that it took the accountant to raise it rather than either of the owners.
sections.workingStyle:
Dean is on site by 6:15 and in the office once a week, on Fridays, which he resents. He works from a tablet in the ute for the site reports and photographs everything, but the tablet is four years old, the camera app crashes, and he keeps a paper site book as the real record because it has never let him down. The office manager has asked him twice to stop doing this.
He talks through problems out loud, usually to whoever is standing nearest, and is at his best with a plan in front of him and a fence line to point at. Reading he is fine with, so long as it is a plan, a soil report, or a spec.
Long written explanations he skims, and he says himself that when he writes a report it comes out "like a text message". The office manager tidies them before they go to clients, which has been going on so long that neither of them mentions it.
He is quick with numbers on site: fall, cut and fill volumes, batter angles, and how many truckloads of spoil, mostly in his head and mostly right. Put the same sums in a spreadsheet and he slows right down and starts second-guessing himself. Reception at the Fleurieu jobs is patchy and he loses signal for hours at a time. Anything he needs during the day he downloads the night before, or it does not exist.
sections.additionalInfo:
Dean coaches under-14s basketball on Wednesday nights and does not miss it. Summer is the busy season and from October to March he works most Saturdays, so any study would need to survive being ignored for five months.
His father-in-law had a stroke in 2025 and Dean does the Sunday driving to appointments. He has not sat an assessment of any kind since the excavator ticket and says he does not much like the idea of being tested on paper for something he does every day.

learners.name: Bree Whitlam
learners.bio: Volunteer fire brigade crew leader of eight years and veterinary nurse, one of two at her brigade trained to take fireground weather observations, requested by name on two campaign fires.
learners.employer: CFS brigade, Kersbrook; mixed practice, Gumeracha

sections.aboutMe: Bree Whitlam is 31 and lives on a small block outside Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills with her partner and two dogs. She is a veterinary nurse at a mixed practice in Gumeracha four days a week, and a volunteer firefighter with her local brigade, where she has served eight years and is now a crew leader.
sections.professionalExperience:
Bree grew up on the block and joined the brigade at twenty-three after the fires came within two paddocks of the house. She holds her basic firefighting and crew leader qualifications through the service, has been on strike teams to the South East and the Mid North, and is one of two people at the brigade trained to take and report field weather observations on the fireground.
Weather is the part she has made her own. She carries a belt weather kit, takes observations at set intervals on any going fire her crew attends, reads the sky and the terrain as well as the instruments, and radios the numbers through to the sector commander. In the last two seasons she has been asked for by name on two campaign fires because the incident controller wanted observations he could trust from the western flank.
Her paid work is veterinary nursing: Certificate IV completed in 2016, surgical and emergency nursing, and she runs the practice's student placements, which means two or three Certificate IV students a year working alongside her for a fortnight each. She writes their placement feedback and has failed one.
sections.careerGoals:
The brigade has put Bree forward as a trainer, which in a volunteer service means teaching new members on Sunday mornings with a manual and a truck. She has been doing it unofficially for three years.
She would like the recognition, partly for herself and partly because she thinks the way new members are currently taught is not good enough and she would have more standing to change it. Her view is that the current approach relies on people already knowing things nobody ever taught them.
She has no plans to leave veterinary nursing and is not looking for the brigade work to turn into a job. She wants to be better at the part of it she has already been doing for three years without a title.
sections.workingStyle:
Bree is precise. Her observation sheets are neat, timed to the minute, and she will re-site the kit rather than record a reading she does not trust. She notices things: the smoke lying flat when it was rising an hour ago, the wind backing before the change comes through, the difference between the ridge and the gully.
She reads and writes well and is comfortable on the radio, which not everyone is. In front of a group she is quieter than she is on the fireground and tends to speak in short sentences and then stop, which she knows and does not much like. She has said she would rather demonstrate something than explain it, and that she runs out of words when people are looking at her.
Her availability is the complication. She works four days at the practice, is on the brigade pager permanently, and in a bad summer will be out three nights a week and gone for four days on a strike team with a day's notice. She cannot tell anyone in advance which weeks those will be.
Internet at Kersbrook is fixed wireless and drops out in the heat, which is exactly when she is busiest. Anything scheduled between December and March will be missed at some point, and she would rather that be planned for than apologised for afterwards.
sections.additionalInfo:
Bree does the brigade's social media and the fundraising quiz night, keeps chickens, and is doing the slow work of putting her block back together after the 2024 fire took the fences.
The block is twenty-five minutes from Gumeracha and fifty from the city, and she does the drive twice a day four days a week, which rules out anything that would need her in Adelaide on a weeknight.
She and her partner are trying for a baby, which she has mentioned to the brigade captain and nobody else.

learners.name: Shannon Delaney
learners.bio: Beauty therapist of sixteen years who writes the salon's treatment room prompt cards, runs the Monday product briefing, and turns over roughly double the salon's average retail without appearing to sell.

sections.aboutMe:
Shannon Delaney is 36 and lives at Seaton with her two primary-school-aged sons. She is a beauty therapist at Halcyon Skin & Body, a nine-room salon at Henley Beach, where she works four days a week and holds the retail floor as well as her treatment room.
She is the only therapist in the salon who has been there more than three years.
sections.professionalExperience:
Shannon trained at nineteen, completed her Diploma of Beauty Therapy in 2010, and has worked in three salons since, with a five-year break running a mobile spray tan and lash business from home while her boys were small. She came back to salon work in 2021.
She does facials, peels, brows and lashes, and the salon's cosmetic tattoo consultations. What sets her apart at Halcyon is product. She is the person the owner sends to the supplier training days, she writes the treatment room prompt cards the other therapists use, and her retail figures are roughly double the salon average without her ever being seen to sell anything.
She keeps a folder of ingredient and contraindication notes she has built herself over fifteen years because, in her words, the supplier sheets tell you what to say and not what to do when the client is on isotretinoin. Two of the junior therapists have photographed pages of it.
She has run the Monday morning product briefing for the salon for about two years, ten minutes standing at the retail shelves with whatever is new, and the owner has stopped calling it anything because it just happens.
sections.careerGoals:
Shannon wants to move into supplier education, running product training for salons, which is a role she has been informally headhunted for twice and turned down because it needed a qualification she does not hold.
She would also take the salon's senior therapist role if it came up, though she is honest that it is the second choice.
She has been out of formal study for sixteen years and is candid that the idea of an assignment makes her feel slightly sick. She asked, at the first conversation, whether there would be exams.
sections.workingStyle:
Shannon is warm and unhurried with clients and can talk product for an hour without it feeling like selling, because she asks first and recommends second. She is the one the junior therapists ask when a client's skin reacts, and she has a good instinct for when to say no to a treatment and the words to say it with.
She works from her phone. Everything is on it: the booking system, the client notes, the product research she does in the ten minutes between clients, and the supplier videos she watches at 2x while the wax heats. She has a laptop that belonged to her ex and it lives in a cupboard. Anything longer than a screen she photographs rather than prints.
Reading dense clinical or regulatory material she finds slow going and says she has to read it three times, though she absorbs the same information easily from a supplier trainer talking over a product. Numbers she is fine with in the salon, retail targets, commission, stock counts, and slower with anything abstract.
Her week is fixed around school hours and one late night on Thursdays. School holidays are the problem: four weeks a year she has no care and works reduced hours, and those weeks move depending on the term dates.
sections.additionalInfo:
Shannon runs the salon's Instagram, does the school's netball club uniforms, and has a standing Sunday with her mother.
Her older son has been assessed with dyslexia in the last year and she has said the process taught her a lot about her own school experience. She mentioned it once, in passing, and did not go further.

learners.name: Marcus Boyle
learners.bio: Leading hand plant operator with eighteen years in civil construction, running a crew of seven, and mentoring two trainees taken on through a mob-specific traineeship.

sections.aboutMe: Marcus Boyle is 41 and lives at Munno Para with his wife and three kids. He is a leading hand plant operator with Ardrossan Civil, working on a subdivision project at Angle Vale after eighteen years in civil construction across roads, subdivisions, and water infrastructure.
sections.professionalExperience:
Marcus started as a pipelayer's labourer at twenty-three, got his tickets over the following decade, and now runs excavator, roller, and skid steer and is the leading hand for a crew of seven. He holds a Certificate III in Civil Construction Plant Operations from 2014.
The leading hand role is mostly communication and he knows it. He takes the daily brief from the site supervisor and turns it into what his crew actually does, runs the prestart, reads the drawings and the service plans and makes sure the crew read them too, and stops the job when the plan and the ground disagree.
He talks to the surveyor, the traffic controllers, the water authority inspector, and the residents who come out to ask why there is an excavator in their court at six in the morning. He negotiates the day-to-day give and take with the other trades on site, which he describes as "half my job and none of my job description".
He has taught three operators to run an excavator properly and can tell within an hour whether someone has been trained or has just been let loose on one.
sections.careerGoals:
Marcus wants to move into a site supervisor role, and the company has told him what everyone in civil gets told: the tickets are not the problem, the paperwork and the qualifications are.
He has also been asked to mentor the two young operators the company took on through a mob-specific traineeship, which he enjoys more than he expected and has no formal grounding in. He has said he does not want to do it badly and would like to know whether what he is doing is right.
sections.workingStyle:
Marcus runs on the radio and on his feet. He is on site at 6, walks the job before the crew arrives, and by seven has told everyone what is happening in language they can use. He is very good in front of the crew, calm with an angry resident, and firm with a subcontractor trying to shortcut a set-down.
Written work is where it slows down. He fills in the prestart and the daily diary because he has to, in short lines, and the supervisor's written instructions he tends to have someone read out or he takes a photo and works through it later in the ute. He says he was "no good at school and got worse", and he learned everything he knows about drawings from a surveyor named Kev who took the time.
He is confident on the phone and the two-way, less so with the tablet the company rolled out for daily diaries last year, and openly says he preferred the paper book. He has worked out enough of the tablet to do his own entries and no more than that.
Site reception at Angle Vale is patchy in the low ground, and the ute is the only place he reliably has signal. Work is 6am to 4pm, sometimes 6, and by the time he gets home the last thing he wants is a screen.
sections.additionalInfo:
Marcus plays and now coaches in the local Aboriginal community footy carnival each year and takes a fortnight off in September for it. He drives his mother to Port Augusta most long weekends.
He has said that the last time anyone asked him to write something down and hand it in was his Certificate III, and that he got through it because the trainer let him talk it out. He remembers the trainer's name.

learners.name: Tyrone Beckett
learners.bio: Haul truck operator on a two-week-on, one-week-off roster who relieves on the dispatch desk, coordinating thirty pieces of equipment across four radio channels on night shift.
learners.employer: Copper mine, Far North SA — FIFO from Adelaide

sections.aboutMe: Tyrone Beckett is 29 and lives at Port Noarlunga with his partner Steph. He is a haul truck operator and dispatch relief on a two-week-on, one-week-off roster at a copper mine in the Far North, flying out of Adelaide, and has been on the same site for four years.
sections.professionalExperience:
Tyrone did two years in a tyre shop after school, then got onto site as a trades assistant at twenty-four and moved to production. He runs haul trucks on nights mostly, and does the prestart inspection on his truck at the start of every shift, which he is unusually thorough about after watching someone else's tyre come apart.
For the last eighteen months he has covered the dispatch desk when the regular operator is on leave, which is where the communication work lives: fleet channel, pit channel, emergency channel, the fleet management system, and the satellite phone when the network drops out. On a night shift he is coordinating between twenty and thirty pieces of equipment and the crib breaks that go with them.
He holds a Certificate II in Surface Extraction Operations and site tickets. The radio work he learned on the job from an operator called Shirl who has been on site twenty years and who, he says, taught him that "the channel is not for chatting and it is not for being clever". He has since passed the same lesson on to two new operators, in almost the same words.
sections.careerGoals:
Tyrone wants the dispatch role permanently, or supervision after that. The company's development pathway wants a qualification behind it and he has been told his existing certificate is not enough for the step up.
He is motivated mainly by the roster. Dispatch is a better swing than nights on a truck, and he and Steph would like to start a family, which he does not think is realistic while he is doing four nights on four off in a camp eight hundred kilometres away.
sections.workingStyle:
Tyrone is disciplined on the radio, which is not universal. He uses the callsign and the format every time, repeats back anything with a number in it, and is the one who tells the new operators to get off the channel.
Twelve-hour night shifts, four on four off within the swing, and by the end of a run of nights he is functional but flat. On his week off he is on Adelaide time and does not want to hear from site, and he means it.
On swing he is in camp with a phone and a shared laptop in the wet mess, and the site network throttles hard in the evening when three hundred people are calling home. Streaming a video is a gamble. He downloads on the bus and works offline, and anything that needs a live connection at a fixed time is effectively unavailable to him.
He reads and writes fine, is unbothered by systems and picks up new software quickly, and prefers a manual he can search to a person explaining. What he dislikes is anything that runs to a schedule, because his schedule is not his, and a week that looks free on paper can turn into six days of covering someone else's leave.
sections.additionalInfo:
Tyrone surfs on his week off and plays in a Wednesday night indoor cricket team he misses two weeks in three. His mother has early-onset Parkinson's and he does the appointments run when he is home, which takes most of a day each swing.
He describes the roster to people as "you get a week off but you also get two weeks of not existing".

learners.name: Riley Fenton
learners.bio: Six months into a carpentry apprenticeship after years of weekend concreting and landscaping work with his uncle, put forward for recognition by an employer on the strength of an offhand remark.

sections.aboutMe: Riley Fenton is 19 and lives at Elizabeth Vale with his mum and younger sister. He started a carpentry apprenticeship in February this year with a small residential builder and is six months in. Before that he was doing warehouse shifts through an agency and helping his uncle on weekends.
sections.professionalExperience:
Riley left school after Year 11. From about fifteen he spent most school holidays and a lot of Saturdays with his uncle Wayne, who runs a one-man concreting and landscaping business, mostly pouring driveways, laying pavers, and building retaining walls around the northern suburbs.
Riley describes it as "helping", which mostly meant barrowing, screeding when he was allowed, cleaning tools, and being told things. He can set out a string line, mix by hand, and knows what a slab looks like when it has been finished properly, none of which he would think to mention unless asked directly.
Between leaving school and starting the apprenticeship he did about eight months of agency warehouse work, some of it nights, in three different sheds.
He has his white card and has done the first block of trade school, where he passed the practical assessments comfortably and scraped through the written ones. His employer put him forward for the recognition process because Riley told him he had "already done heaps of this stuff" with his uncle.
On the current job he is mostly on clean-up, cutting to a mark, and carrying, and he has been allowed to fix off a small amount of framing under supervision. He has not been shown how to set out anything himself yet.
sections.careerGoals:
Riley wants to finish his trade and eventually work for himself, which he says because his uncle does and it looks alright from where he is standing.
Nearer term he wants to stop being the one who sweeps up. He is doing the recognition process because his boss suggested it and he is not entirely sure what it involves, and he has not asked.
sections.workingStyle:
Riley is willing and physically capable and turns up on time, which his boss rates highly. He learns by watching and copying and is uncomfortable asking questions in front of the other blokes, so he tends to guess and then get corrected, which he takes well but which costs time.
He reads slowly and avoids it. Trade school assessments he has been doing at his mum's kitchen table on his phone because the laptop from school stopped working and has not been replaced, and he has already had one extension. Typing on the phone is slow enough that his answers come out shorter than he means them to.
He is quick with anything hands-on and remembers a sequence after being shown twice, but written explanations of things he can do go nowhere. Nobody has ever asked him to write down what he did on a job, and when it was suggested he looked at it as though it were a trick.
When asked for evidence he produced a phone gallery, some of it his and some of it his uncle's, mostly finished work with nobody in the shot and no dates he could vouch for. He was surprised that this might not be enough and did not know what else there could be.
He answers questions in a few words and then waits. Asked the same question a second way, or asked to show rather than say, he will talk for as long as anyone wants.
sections.additionalInfo:
Riley plays basketball on Monday nights and drops his sister at school before work, which means a 6:20 start is tight and he has been late twice.
He does not have a car of his own and uses his mum's or gets a lift from a workmate. Money is tight on first-year wages and he has said he will not be paying for anything toward the qualification himself. His mum has asked twice how it is going and he has told her it is fine.

learners.name: Nadia Kirilenko
learners.bio: Senior claims consultant handling escalated home and contents claims, who does the call coaching for a team of nine and takes the calls that arrive needing Ukrainian or Russian.
learners.employer: Chalmers Rowe Insurance — Mile End contact centre

sections.aboutMe: Nadia Kirilenko is 34 and lives at Mawson Lakes with her husband and her father, who moved in after her mother died in 2024. She is a senior claims consultant at Chalmers Rowe Insurance, a mid-sized general insurer with a contact centre at Mile End, where she has worked for six years and now handles the escalated home and contents claims.
sections.professionalExperience:
Nadia came to Australia from Ukraine at eleven and did all her schooling here. She went into a phone role at nineteen at a telco, moved to banking collections in her twenties, and into insurance claims in 2020, which she says is the first job she has had where being kind to people on the worst day of their year is actually the job.
Her queue is the claims that have gone wrong somewhere: a delayed assessor, a disputed exclusion, a repair that has failed twice, or a customer who has been passed between four people. She takes the call, works out what has actually happened by reading back through the file, tells the customer the truth about it including when the answer is no, and owns it to resolution.
She takes the difficult calls off the newer consultants and does the call coaching for her team of nine, which means sitting with a recording, marking up what she would have done differently, and going through it with the consultant afterwards. Two team leaders have told her she is better at it than they are.
No qualification beyond Year 12 and a Tier 1 general insurance compliance accreditation she completed internally in 2021.
sections.careerGoals:
Nadia has been acting team leader twice and wants it permanently. The last recruitment round went to an external candidate with a diploma and she was told, in a development conversation she describes as "polite and unmistakable", that her file needed something on it.
She is doing this for the promotion and is unsentimental about that. She has also said that a team leader role would mean fixed hours and no overtime, which matters to her for reasons that have nothing to do with her career.
sections.workingStyle:
Nadia is organised and fast on the systems: the claims platform, the telephony, the knowledge base, and three spreadsheets of her own that the team uses. Her call notes are the ones other consultants copy the structure of, and she keeps a paper notebook beside the keyboard for the live call because typing while listening splits her attention.
She speaks Ukrainian and Russian and takes the calls that come through needing either, which she is quietly proud of and which is not in her position description or her pay. She has an ear for a customer who is not following and slows down without making a point of it.
Her working hours are fixed: 8:30 to 4:30 so she can be home for her father, who has moderate dementia and cannot be alone in the late afternoon. She has a respite worker Tuesday and Thursday afternoons and that is the only reliable window she has for anything other than work.
She reads quickly and writes well, though English is her second language and she still occasionally reaches for the wrong preposition, which she notices and other people do not. She dislikes video content, finds it slow, and would rather have a document she can skim and come back to at the part she needs.
sections.additionalInfo:
Nadia does the shopping and appointments for her father and has not taken more than four consecutive days of leave since 2024. She swims at the Mawson Lakes pool at 6am, which is the only hour of the day that belongs to her.
She has said, once, in a development conversation, that she is worried about what happens to her career if her father gets worse.

learners.name: Jonty Fairweather
learners.bio: Bar supervisor at a forty-seat cocktail bar who runs the open, the service, the close, the stock, and two juniors, and wrote the close-down list the bar works to.

sections.aboutMe: Jonty Fairweather is 27 and shares a flat in the East End with two housemates. He is the bar supervisor at Corriedale, a small cocktail bar off Vardon Avenue with forty seats, a back bar of about three hundred bottles, and a menu that changes twice a year.
sections.professionalExperience:
Jonty glassied at nineteen in a suburban hotel, worked three years in a high-volume city pub, and came to Corriedale five years ago as a bartender. He has been supervisor for two, which means he runs the bar on the nights the owner is not there: the open, the service, the close, the stock, and the two juniors.
The close is his. Corriedale does not have a cleaner; the bar team does it, and Jonty wrote the close-down list the bar works to. That covers the glass washer strip and clean, the beer lines, the ice well and the drainage, the back bar and the speed rails, the public side including the tables and the floor, and the waste and recycling out to the bins in the laneway.
He is the one who deals with the gas bottles for the taps and is careful about it in a way the juniors initially found funny and no longer do. He orders the spirits, counts the stock on a Monday, and works out what the menu change will cost before he takes it to the owner.
He has his RSA, a food safety certificate, and no other qualifications. He has placed in two national cocktail competitions.
sections.careerGoals:
Jonty wants his own small bar, which he says the way everyone in hospitality says it, but he has a spreadsheet and a location in mind so it may be more than talk.
Nearer term he has been approached about a venue manager role at a larger group and the recruiter told him the group wants qualifications for anyone signing off on compliance. He is also quietly aware that his back is not going to do this forever, and that the people he started with are mostly not in the industry any more.
He has never applied for anything with a written application and would not know where to start with one. The recruiter approached him because of the competition results.
sections.workingStyle:
Jonty is meticulous behind the bar in a way that does not look like effort. Everything has a place, the speed rail is set up the same every night, and he cannot walk past a smeared glass. He is fast, chatty, and very good with a room, and he trains the juniors by making them do it rather than by explaining, which works about two thirds of the time.
His hours are the problem for everything else. He starts at four and finishes at two, later on a Friday and Saturday, gets home at three, and sleeps until eleven. He is unavailable to the entire daytime world and has missed a dentist appointment three times. Monday and Tuesday are his weekend.
Reading he is fine with. He devours drinks books and reads the chemistry of things for fun, and will follow a technical article on clarification without blinking. Anything administrative he leaves until the last possible moment and then does it well and at speed, which he knows is a habit and not a strategy.
He works off his phone and a tablet in the office at the venue, has no printer, and says the last time he owned a laptop was at school. The flat has decent internet but two housemates on shift work, and the only quiet time in it is the middle of the day when he is asleep.
He drinks less than people assume and has been sober on shift for two years, which he mentions unprompted.
sections.additionalInfo:
Jonty enters cocktail competitions two or three times a year, which eats his days off for about a month each time.
He has a full sleeve and a hand tattoo, which cost him a job once and which he mentions as a reason he ended up in the kind of venue that does not care. His mum is in Whyalla and he goes up every second month, driving after a Sunday close.
